title: Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say
gist: Dharma-AI analyzed 272 production supervised fine-tuning jobs (~7,382 GPU-hours on shared NVIDIA H200 clusters) and found the standard 6·P·D FLOP estimate explains little of wall-clock time (R² 0.31, MAE 12.41 h), while a CatBoost regressor using only pre-dispatch config features reaches R² 0.98 and MAE 1.71 h. The gap is driven by non-compute overheads — evaluation cadence, checkpoint I/O, setup and multi-tenant contention — which matter for GPU scheduling and utilization economics.

insights.claim: On shared GPU clusters, inaccurate job-duration estimates directly waste scarce capacity: jobs finishing early leave GPUs idle until the next dispatch, and jobs running late push back everything queued behind them.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Duration prediction is a lever on GPU utilization and therefore on effective cost per GPU-hour for any AI compute operator.
insights.quote: When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips
insights.locator: GPUs are among the most expensive

insights.claim: Most teams estimate fine-tuning duration with a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation, which can say nine hours for a job that actually finishes the next afternoon.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Suggests systematic under-utilization and planning slippage in AI training operations that rely on compute-only math.
insights.quote: It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

insights.claim: An accurate pre-dispatch duration predictor lets a scheduler decide which jobs to co-schedule, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will meet its deadline.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Watch for ML-based scheduling/orchestration tooling as a value-add layer for GPU cloud and cluster-management vendors.

insights.claim: The standard dense-Transformer estimate T = 6·P·D / (N_GPU · FLOPS_peak · MFU) models only the optimization loop, and MFU typically sits between 30% and 60% with the right value unknown in advance.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Compute-only capacity planning carries a wide inherent error band even before non-compute overheads are counted.
insights.quote: MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance

insights.claim: Real fine-tuning jobs include large non-compute overheads — environment setup, model download and loading, tokenization, periodic evaluations, checkpoint uploads and final upload to object storage — which compete for network and storage I/O on multi-tenant clusters.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Storage and network I/O, not just GPU FLOPs, determine effective training throughput — relevant to storage/networking suppliers for AI clusters.

insights.claim: Two fine-tuning jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart because overheads depend on configuration and do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Nominal compute is a poor proxy for job cost; pricing or chargeback based on FLOPs alone will be mispriced.
insights.quote: Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

insights.claim: Across 272 SFT runs, the best FLOP baseline (MFU 30%) achieved only R² 0.31 and MAE 12.41 h, while MFU 45% gave R² 0.18 and MFU 60% gave R² 0.01; sweeping MFU from 0.25 to 0.65 never fixed it.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Tuning a single utilization constant cannot rescue compute-only estimates.
insights.quote: No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline.

insights.claim: Calculon, a detailed analytical LLM training performance model (Isaev et al., SC '23) extended to cover LoRA, GQA, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU, scored R² −0.51 and its estimates corresponded to a median of only 11% of observed wall-clock time.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Shows roughly 89% of a production fine-tuning job's wall-clock time can fall outside the optimization step that analytical models capture.
insights.quote: Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time.

insights.claim: The authors argue Calculon's failure is not a flaw as a step-level tool but evidence of how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Efficiency gains may come more from fixing pipeline overheads than from kernel/MFU optimization.
insights.quote: It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

insights.claim: A CatBoost regressor using only information available before dispatch reached R² 0.98, MAE 1.71 h and median absolute error 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation on 272 SFT jobs totaling about 7,382 H200 GPU-hours.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Order-of-magnitude error reduction (12.41 h to 1.71 h MAE) makes tight GPU bin-packing feasible.

insights.claim: Linear Regression and Ridge improved on FLOP baselines (Ridge MAE 7.23 h, R² 0.73) but stalled, while XGBoost (R² 0.97, MAE 1.95 h) and CatBoost were within one standard deviation of each other, indicating strongly nonlinear configuration-duration relationships.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Gradient boosting on job logs is a cheap, practical approach any cluster operator can replicate.
insights.quote: Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting.
insights.locator: Linear models help, and then stall

insights.claim: The predictor feeds the FLOP estimate (MFU fixed at 0.45) in as one feature, so the model starts from the compute-only number and learns corrections from overhead-exposing features like num_eval_data, num_saves and num_params_saved.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: A hybrid analytical-plus-learned design pattern applicable to other infrastructure cost forecasting problems.

insights.claim: 80% of out-of-fold predictions fell within 2.20 h and 90% within 4.31 h; median error stayed about one hour or less up to 60-hour jobs but rose to 5.19 h (P90 18.51 h) for the 13 runs above 60 hours.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Long-running jobs remain the hardest to schedule; more data on long runs is the key gap.

insights.claim: On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE dropped from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when training data increased from 85% to 100% of the partition, with no clear plateau, implying more production logs should keep improving accuracy.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Operators with larger job histories gain a compounding data advantage in scheduling accuracy.

insights.claim: num_eval_data — total samples processed in evaluation over a job's life — was the single most important feature in the CatBoost model, ahead of trainable parameters, eval batch size, total params and GPU-scaled train batch.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Evaluation cadence is a hidden cost driver in fine-tuning; trimming it is a low-effort GPU-hour saving.

insights.claim: Evaluation frequency, evaluation set size and number of checkpoints persisted all shape wall-clock time, and these are choices often made by habit when writing training configs.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Config hygiene (eval/checkpoint policy) is an underexploited lever on fine-tuning cost.
insights.quote: These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.
insights.locator: Feature importance is not a causal

insights.claim: SHAP analysis showed high evaluation volume consistently increases predicted time, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Model size drives cost mostly at the high end; for small/mid models, overheads dominate.

insights.claim: Larger GPU allocations showed positive contributions to predicted time only because bigger allocations correlate with bigger jobs; num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale, not evidence that more GPUs slow jobs.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Caution when reading feature-importance outputs as causal in infrastructure analytics.
insights.quote: It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.
insights.locator: One caveat on reading the plots

insights.claim: The dataset covers SFT only on NVIDIA H200 GPUs (1, 2 or 4 GPUs from an 8–32 GPU pool across 1–4 nodes), model families up to 15B parameters, both LoRA and full fine-tuning, on Hugging Face Transformers and Unsloth stacks, with durations from 1.6 to 172.4 hours.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Results are calibrated to H200 infrastructure and small/mid models; transfer to other GPU generations requires retraining.

insights.claim: The fitted model should not be expected to transfer numerically to other GPU generations without retraining; a mixed-pool predictor would need hardware descriptors like compute throughput, memory bandwidth and interconnect topology.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Heterogeneous GPU fleets (mixing generations/vendors) make scheduling harder — an opening for hardware-aware scheduling software.

insights.claim: Dharma-AI plans to extend the work with hardware-specific descriptors, validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for sparse configurations, other training objectives like RLHF/DPO/RLVR, and more long-run data; the full paper is coming to arXiv.
insights.speaker: Bruno Duarte
insights.so_what: Watch the arXiv paper for a reusable pipeline that could become a feature in cluster schedulers.
